historical_timeline.summary: Her father dies of brain cancer.
Original cast member of Saturday Night Live; bouts of bulimia in these years.
Marries Gene Wilder; they try to have a child.
Severe fatigue begins and is attributed to Epstein-Barr virus.
After about ten months of bloating, pain and wrong diagnoses, diagnosed with stage IV ovarian cancer; surgery, then chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
The cancer returns after a remission.
Dies at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, at 42.
Her husband speaks about the delay in her diagnosis; registry, detection center and Gilda's Club founded in her name.

claims.statement: Gilda Radner was born on June 28, 1946, into a prosperous Detroit Jewish family; her paternal grandfather had emigrated from Lithuania.

claims.statement: She was the first person cast in Saturday Night Live, performed with its original troupe from 1975 to 1980, won an Emmy Award in 1978, and made several films, including three with Gene Wilder, whom she married in 1984.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her work as a comedian and actor anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: Her father died of brain cancer when she was fourteen. Her grandmother, a cousin, and an aunt had all had ovarian cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history only. A strong family history of ovarian cancer is the reason the modern episode offers germline testing at diagnosis.

claims.statement: Her illness began with severe fatigue, which sources date to the filming of Haunted Honeymoon in England in 1985 or to early 1986; her internist attributed it to Epstein-Barr virus and told her not to worry.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The start of the ten months of symptoms before her diagnosis; the anchor for the presenting problem in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Over the following months she had bloating so marked that she could barely button her trousers, cramps and pelvic pain, fevers, and shaking legs; one doctor thought it was depression and another constipation, and gynecologists said the cramps were nothing to worry about. In her memoir she wrote that she now had 'Epstein-Barr virus and mittelschmerz.' It was ten months from her first symptoms before ovarian cancer was found, and the CA-125 blood test was never done.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The diagnostic delay that the modern episode teaches against: persistent bloating, pelvic pain and early satiety in a woman of 40 meet the ovarian cancer symptom index and call for a pelvic examination, a transvaginal ultrasound and a CA-125.

claims.statement: She was diagnosed with stage IV ovarian cancer in October 1986; surgery removed a tumor the size of a grapefruit, and chemotherapy and radiation therapy followed.

claims.statement: Before her illness she and her husband tried to have a child; she had two miscarriages, one during the filming of Haunted Honeymoon in London, and an unsuccessful round of in vitro fertilization, after which doctors told her she was infertile.

claims.statement: During treatment she found emotional support at The Wellness Community, through the psychotherapist Joanna Bull, and wrote her autobiography, It's Always Something, between chemotherapy treatments; it was published in 1989. After a remission, her cancer returned in December 1988.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Support during treatment is part of the modern survivorship plan.

claims.statement: In May 1989 she was admitted to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles for a CT scan, did not regain consciousness after sedation, and died there three days later, on May 20, 1989, at 42.

claims.statement: After her death, Gilda's Club was founded in her honor by Gene Wilder, Joanna Bull and Joel Siegel, with the first clubhouse opening in 1995; it later merged with The Wellness Community to form the Cancer Support Community. Wilder testified to a House subcommittee about ovarian cancer, a detection center at Cedars-Sinai was named for her, and in 1990 the familial ovarian cancer registry at Roswell Park was named for her.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her legacy in early detection, hereditary risk and cancer support, which the modern episode reflects.

claims.statement: After her death her husband said that no doctor had asked about her family history of ovarian cancer, and wrote that her cancer might have been caught in time if her doctors had given her the CA-125 blood test or asked about that history, and that she 'didn't have to die.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective, personal reading after her death; whether earlier diagnosis would have changed the outcome cannot be known. The teaching point rests on the delay itself.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize ovarian cancer early in a woman of 39 with persistent bloating, early fullness, and pelvic pain, the symptoms that went unexplained for ten months in Gilda Radner's life: apply the ovarian cancer symptom index (Goff), examine the abdomen and pelvis, and order a CA-125 and a transvaginal ultrasound at the first visit; CT staging and an image-guided biopsy within the week; prompt gynecologic oncology care with primary cytoreductive surgery aiming for no visible residual disease; carboplatin and paclitaxel with antiemetic, neuropathy and blood-count monitoring and extended thromboprophylaxis; germline genetic counseling and testing for every woman with epithelial ovarian cancer, with tumor testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2; PARP inhibitor maintenance chosen from the tumor result; and survivorship care with distress screening and peer support, on the NCCN ovarian cancer guideline, the ASCO germline and somatic testing and PARP inhibitor guidelines, and ACOG Committee Opinion 716.

Suspected ovarian cancer; transvaginal ultrasound, CT, CA-125 and gynecologic oncology review booked within the week

The transvaginal ultrasound the next day showed solid and cystic masses in both ovaries with ascites; CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis the day after that showed omental and peritoneal disease without spread to the liver, lungs or lymph nodes; and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the omentum two days later shows high-grade serous carcinoma of Mullerian origin. She says she is frightened but relieved to have an answer within a week. She had genetic counseling this afternoon. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.
